newsitem.title: USA: Key senator undecided on chemical weapons treaty. [CORRECTED 22:09 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Key senator undecided on chemical weapons treaty. [CORRECTED 22:09 GMT]

text.p: A key senator said on Sunday he still had not made up his mind whether to vote for a treaty outlawing chemical weapons as President Bill Cliton launched an all-out lobbying blitz to gain Senate approval.

For the first time in 29 years, both the U.S. Secretary of State and Defense Secretary appeared together on NBC's "Meet the Press" program to make the case for the treaty. The last time there was such a joint appearance was when President Lyndon Johnson wanted to drum up support for the Vietnam War.

Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and Defense Secretary William Cohen conceded that the outlook for required Senate approval of the treaty remained uncertain ahead of a debate on it scheduled for Wednesday.
Albright argued that failure to approve it would harm U.S. credibility. "We will be in the same position as Iraq and Libya," she said of two non-signatories to the treaty.

But Trent Lott, the Senate Republican Majority Leader whose vote is critical to Clinton's chances of winning approval, said on the CNN program 'Late Edition With Frank Sesno' (corrects program from "CNN Live") that he was waiting to see what conditions are attached to the measure before deciding whether to support it.
"I'll have to look at the final product," he said.
Lott said a provision that allows sharing of information with other signatories was "a fundamental flaw."
"That is the critical point for me," he said, suggesting that a country like Iraq could learn how the United States would protect its troops from chemical warfare by reviewing U.S. formulas.
The Senate was to debate the Chemical Weapons Convention on Wednesday and supporters give it a 50-50 chance, with Lott and undecided Republicans holding the key.
The pact was negotiated by the Ronald Reagan and George Bush administrations but Clinton has made it a cause of his own.
On Friday, Clinton told reporters that there was no such thing as perfect verifiability but the treaty's tough standards would detect militarily significant cheating.
Clinton denied the treaty would require the United States to share its advanced chemical defense technology.

Jesse Helms, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, has offered provisions that would effectively bar U.S. participation in the treaty when it goes into effect on April 29, with or without the United States.
Treaty supporters are trying to kill these so-called killer amendments.
The treaty was signed in 1993 and more than 70 countries have ratified it.
